clinicalPearls: Recluse spider bites can cause a locally necrotic skin lesion (cutaneous loxoscelism) and, less often, a systemic (viscerocutaneous) illness
The lesion often evolves over days from an erythematous area to a central blister and then a dark eschar with surrounding pallor and redness
Systemic loxoscelism can include haemolysis, disseminated intravascular coagulation and acute kidney injury, more often in children
Definitive diagnosis is difficult because the spider is rarely captured and many necrotic lesions are wrongly blamed on spiders
Most cutaneous lesions heal with supportive wound care alone
Because presentation overlaps with infection, careful reassessment is needed before attributing necrosis to a spider
reference.pathophysiology: Recluse spider venom contains sphingomyelinase D, which damages cell membranes and activates complement and neutrophils, producing local dermonecrosis and, when venom effects are systemic, intravascular haemolysis and a coagulopathy. The characteristic necrotic ulcer results from vascular injury, thrombosis and inflammatory tissue destruction at the bite site. Systemic loxoscelism reflects widespread red-cell membrane injury and immune activation.
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial skin and soft-tissue infection or abscess
Cutaneous anthrax or other necrotic infections
Vasculitis or other causes of skin necrosis
additionalInvestigations: Serial wound examination and documentation of lesion evolution
Full blood count and haemolysis markers where systemic illness is suspected
Coagulation studies and renal function in suspected viscerocutaneous loxoscelism
Microbiological assessment to exclude infective mimics
redFlags: Haemolysis, dark urine or falling haemoglobin
Features of disseminated intravascular coagulation or acute kidney injury
Rapidly spreading necrosis or systemic sepsis suggesting necrotising infection
reference.prognosis: Most cutaneous cases heal over weeks with supportive care, though large lesions may scar; systemic loxoscelism is uncommon but can be serious, particularly in children.
pitfalls: Diagnosing a spider bite for any necrotic ulcer without a confirmed exposure
Missing a necrotising soft-tissue infection masquerading as loxoscelism
Overlooking systemic haemolysis, especially in children
Performing early aggressive surgery on an evolving lesion
management: Manage most cutaneous lesions with supportive wound care, cleansing, analgesia, elevation and tetanus prophylaxis, allowing the eschar to demarcate before any debridement
Delay surgical debridement or reconstruction until the necrotic lesion has fully declared, as early excision worsens outcomes
Monitor for systemic (viscerocutaneous) loxoscelism with serial haemolysis markers, coagulation studies and renal function, particularly in children
Treat systemic disease supportively with intravenous fluids, transfusion for significant haemolysis, and management of disseminated intravascular coagulation and acute kidney injury
Reassess to exclude infective mimics before attributing necrosis to a spider, and treat secondary infection if it develops
Escalate to critical care for severe haemolysis, coagulopathy or renal failure
